limits: Illustrative case study for one fictional insurer, with no measured results, data sizes or benchmarks.
Depends on earlier chapters (type 1/2/3 SCD, minidimensions, bridges, heterogeneous products) which are not restated in full.
Claimant and third-party dimensions are described as dirty and hard to track across claims; no cleansing method given.
Only policy and claims processes covered; investment, HR, finance and purchasing excluded.
practices: Handle all policy transactions as one business process and fact table, splitting into quoting/rating/underwriting tables only if needed (p.308).

Build both a transaction fact table and a monthly periodic snapshot for pay-in-advance revenue; source earned premium from the operational revenue-recognition system rather than re-deriving it (p.308, 317).
Implement role-playing dates (transaction date, effective date) as views over one physical date table with unique column names (p.310).
Use type 1 for corrections (date of birth), type 2 for ZIP code, type 3 for en masse segment realignment (p.310-311).
Move closely monitored, fast-changing attributes of large dimensions (policyholder, covered item) to a minidimension keyed from the fact table (p.312).
Use a bridge table (SIC group, insured driver) for multivalued attributes, with a weighting factor and optional begin/end dates, plus an Unknown row (p.312, 318).
Treat coverage limits and deductibles as facts, and keep textual descriptions in dimensions (p.312-313).
Keep policy number as a degenerate dimension when header attributes live in other dimensions (p.313).
Add an audit key to each fact row linking to extract time, source table and software version (p.314).
Handle heterogeneous lines with custom dimension tables per line of business, without custom fact tables for transactions (p.314-315).
Conform dimensions (identical or subsets) and facts (same definition or different names) across fact tables (p.316, 329).
Replace the daily date with a month dimension and transaction type with a status dimension in the snapshot (p.316).
Build a consolidated fact table of premium and claim metrics only after the base models are delivered (p.324).
Use a factless fact table with a count fixed at 1 for accident events; bridge tables optional to keep grain (p.325).
Keep the bus matrix at high-level business processes in planning; list each fact table, grain and facts in the implementation matrix (p.320-321).

Avoid mistakes: text in fact tables; skimping on verbose dimension attributes; snowflaking hierarchies; ignoring attribute change; hardware-only fixes (use aggregates); smart keys instead of integer surrogate keys; ignoring grain; report-driven design; normalized presentation; non-conformed facts and dimensions (p.326-329).

terms.definition: Coverages can be considered the products sold by the insurance company.
the house, the car, or other specific insured item
a preliminary estimate of the insurance company's eventual liability for the claim
selling the rights to further recoveries to specialists at a discount to get cash immediately and close the books on the claim
written is revenue sold in a month; earned is revenue recognised as coverage is provided
a fact table that combines data from multiple business processes
ensuring technical definitions of a fact match exactly across data marts, else they are not both called the same name
the collision of keys at a point in space and time, with a fact always valued at 1 for counting
